sections.title: Wound healing
sections.digest:
Injury sets off an ordered cascade that ends in a healed wound. **Three components** share in every wound, but their proportion and timing differ by wound type: **contraction** (myofibroblasts containing the smooth-muscle protein actin; starts at once, runs 2–3 weeks), **granulation tissue formation** (later replaced by fibrous tissue), and **epithelialisation**. A clean sutured wound epithelialises in ~48 h with little contraction/granulation; when edges are wide apart, contraction and granulation dominate and epithelium only covers once the gap is filled.

**Three phases:**
- **Haemostasis & inflammation (~5 days):** platelets adhere to subendothelial collagen and trigger the coagulation cascade; released cytokines/growth factors draw in leucocytes, macrophages and lymphocytes. Macrophages phagocytose, debride, and release growth factors that recruit fibroblasts and endothelial cells.
- **Proliferation:** fibroblasts secrete collagen; endothelial buds from intact venules + fibroblasts form granulation tissue; epithelial cells advance from wound edges and islands. Young epithelium is thinner and lacks sebaceous glands, sweat glands and hair follicles.
- **Maturation & remodelling (~1 year):** collagen III is laid down first, then replaced as collagen I rises; fibres thicken and align along lines of stress, raising tensile strength. A wound **never regains full original strength**.

**Types of healing:** **primary** (clean, immediately closed → minimal fibrosis, neat scar); **secondary** (edges not approximated / gaping from infection → granulation infill, ugly scar); **tertiary = delayed primary** (contaminated wound left open ~5 days, then delayed primary sutures if no infection).
highYield: 3 weeks → 20% of final strength; 3 months → 80% of original strength; never regains full strength.
Collagen III is deposited first, then replaced by collagen I during remodelling.
Contraction is driven by myofibroblasts (contain actin).
Tertiary intention = delayed primary closure of a contaminated wound after ~5 days.
Growth factors of healing: PDGF, TNF-α, IL-1, FGF.

sections.title: Types of wounds
sections.digest:
**Closed wounds:** **contusion** (blunt blow → capillary extravasation; painful, swollen; bluish → brown/green; elevate + anti-inflammatory ointment) and **haematoma** (heavy bleeding; cystic → clots within hours → liquefies; small = aspirate with wide-bore needle, otherwise surgical evacuation under asepsis).

**Open wounds:**
- **Abrasion** — superficial layers scraped by friction; very painful (exposed nerve endings); clean with a bland antiseptic + non-adherent dressing.
- **Incised** — sharp object; longer than deep, clean edges, little tissue destruction; extensive haemorrhage; tendons/nerves liable to be cut.
- **Lacerated** — blunt violence/RTA; irregular, devascularised, contaminated; high infection risk; inflammatory oedema raises tension → secondary ischaemia; often a **degloving** injury.
- **Penetrating** — pointed object; **deeper than long**; small opening + poor drainage → infection; deceptive — may miss an injured viscus.
- **Missile** — bullet transfers high kinetic energy; **KE = MV²/2g**, so high-velocity rifles are far more serious than pistols. Damage from direct track injury, shock waves, temporary cavitation, and bone fragments acting as secondary missiles.
- **Bites** — animal or human; lacerated + contaminated; high infection incidence.
highYield: Penetrating wounds are deeper than long — always suspect deep-structure injury.
Missile kinetic energy = MV²/2g; velocity dominates over mass.
In missile injury, structures far from the tract may be damaged.
Small haematoma → wide-bore needle aspiration; large → surgical evacuation.

sections.title: Management of open wounds
sections.digest:
**First aid:** follow multiple-injury priorities; ask timing and cause (predict injured structures — a femoral-triangle stab risks the femoral vessels); **tetanus prophylaxis**; prophylactic antibiotics (add **anaerobic cover** in deep/lacerated wounds); stop bleeding by **direct compression** (sterile dressing + tight bandage; tourniquet only as a temporary measure before theatre); suspected fracture → plain X-ray + splint; feel distal pulses — **urgent duplex if absent**.

**In theatre:** thorough **saline irrigation** + meticulous foreign-body removal + antiseptic (povidone-iodine); repair a major artery/vein, ligate small vessels; nerves/tendons — repair in clean incised wounds but **defer in contaminated** ones; clean incised muscle → mattress sutures, and **excise necrotic muscle** (dark red/grey, no contraction when pinched, no bleeding when cut); in contaminated or extensively destroyed wounds **leave the deep fascia open**. Skin: clean & early (<6 h) → primary closure; contaminated/late → delayed primary; lacerations → debride to healthy tissue; degloving of doubtful viability → **second look at 3–4 days**. Associated fracture with infection risk → **external fixation** (internal fixation would spread infection to bone). **All missile injuries require exploration.**
highYield: Contaminated wound rule: no nerve repair, no tendon repair, don't close the deep fascia, don't close the skin.
Clean & early skin (<6 h) → primary closure; contaminated/late → delayed primary.
Necrotic muscle: dark red/grey, no contraction when pinched, no bleeding when cut — excise it.
Associated fracture + infection risk → external fixation (internal spreads infection to bone).
Tourniquet is only a temporary bridge to theatre.

tables.title: Skin decision in the open wound

pitfalls: In contaminated wounds, deferring nerve/tendon repair and leaving fascia + skin open is correct — not negligence.

sections.title: Chronic wounds
sections.digest:
Chronic wounds fail the normal acute sequence within a reasonable time (~3 months), arrested at the inflammatory/proliferative phases with minimal contraction and collagen. They share **local hypoxia** (ischaemia, trauma, vasculitis); manage the **general and local factors together**.

**Three frequent categories:**
- **Chronic leg ulcers** — an ulcer is a break in epithelial/mucosal continuity. Commonest is the **venous** ulcer; others are ischaemic, neuropathic, and neoplastic (SCC or, rarely, BCC).
- **Diabetic foot ulcers.**
- **Pressure sores** (decubitus ulcers) — in bedridden patients from sustained skin pressure. **Risk:** old age, poor nutrition, anaemia, denervation, paraplegia, ICU stay, immobilisation, soiling by stool/urine. **Sites:** ischial tuberosity, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleoli. **Stages:** erythema → partial-thickness loss → full-thickness loss short of fascia → deeper destruction (muscle, bone, joints). **Prevention/treatment:** correct general factors + skilled nursing (regular turning), keep skin dry, air mattresses, regular debridement + **VAC**, and rotation/myocutaneous/fasciocutaneous **flaps**.
highYield: Chronic wound = fails to heal within ~3 months.
Commonest chronic leg ulcer is venous.
Pressure-sore stages: erythema → partial-thickness → full-thickness short of fascia → muscle/bone/joint.
Pressure sores favour the ischial tuberosity, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleoli.

sections.title: Suture materials
sections.digest:
Sutures approximate wound edges until healing occurs. Classified by **origin** (natural/synthetic), **absorption** (absorbable/non-absorbable — the most important factor), and **synthesis** (monofilament vs multifilament/braided). Natural materials provoke more tissue reaction and can maintain infection; **multifilament** sutures react more and pick up **~10× more organisms** than an equivalent monofilament (capillary spaces between filaments harbour bacteria).

**Absorbable:** **chromic catgut** (absorbed ~3 weeks; loses 50–80% strength in 2 weeks; GI/urinary tract; uncommon in modern practice), **polyglycolic acid / Dexon** (multifilament, good tensile, absorbed 2–3 months), **polyglactin / Vicryl** (multifilament, absorption ~4 months per the book; GI anastomoses), **polydioxanone / PDS** (monofilament, loses 50% tensile at 6 weeks, **slowest absorbable**).

**Non-absorbable:** **silk** (protein → marked reaction; multifilament; easy handling; remove if infected; loses 40% strength at 6 weeks — in fact very slowly absorbable), **nylon / polyamide** (mono or multifilament; good tensile; knot not very secure), **polypropylene / Prolene** (monofilament; inert — no need to remove even if infected; difficult knotting; **ideal for abdominal closure and hernia repair**), **stainless steel** (very high tensile, very inert, difficult handling; sternotomy closure). **Other skin closure:** clips, staplers, adhesive tapes (no reaction), skin glue.
highYield: Absorption is the most important classifier of a suture.
PDS is the slowest-absorbing absorbable suture.
Prolene is ideal for abdominal wound closure and hernia repair.
A multifilament suture picks up ~10× more organisms than an equivalent monofilament.
Stainless steel is used to close a sternotomy.

PDS is the slowest absorbable; don't confuse 'loses 50% tensile at 6 weeks' with full absorption.

sections.title: Wound dressings
sections.digest:
Dressings provide the ideal healing environment and prevent bacterial overgrowth.

- **Occlusive** (gauze + adhesive plaster): protect and prevent evaporation → maintain hydration; local hypoxia stimulates capillary proliferation and autolysis of slough. **Not** for infected or highly exudative wounds.
- **Semi-occlusive:** permeable to water vapour and gases, impermeable to bacteria; hydrocolloid sheets give a moist bed.
- **Alginates** (from seaweed): form a fibrous gel on contact with exudate → moist environment.
- **Osmotic agents** (Debrisan, urea crystals, honey): absorb exudate.
- **Healing enhancers:** **VAC** (negative pressure → more granulation + wound contraction; good results in bed sores and diabetic ulcers) and increased local hydration (moist healing).
highYield: Occlusive dressings are unsuitable for infected or highly exudative wounds.
VAC (negative pressure) boosts granulation and contraction — useful in bed sores and diabetic ulcers.
Alginates come from seaweed and gel with exudate.
Semi-occlusive dressings are permeable to gases/vapour but not bacteria.

mcqs.stem: Which cell is chiefly responsible for wound contraction?

options.why: Contains the smooth-muscle protein actin and pulls wound edges together.
A first-responder of acute inflammation; it does not contract the wound.
Debrides and releases growth factors, but does not physically contract the wound.
Forms new capillaries (granulation), not contraction.
Drives epithelialisation, a separate component from contraction.

explanation: Contraction is produced by myofibroblasts, which contain actin.
It begins at once and runs over 2–3 weeks.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Contraction is a myofibroblast/actin phenomenon.

mcqs.stem: Which collagen type predominates first in a healing wound?

options.why: Laid down rapidly in the proliferative phase to bridge the gap.
Predominates only later, after remodelling replaces type III.
A cartilage collagen, not central to skin wound healing.
A basement-membrane collagen, not the provisional wound matrix.
A minor collagen; not the one that predominates early.

explanation: Type III collagen is deposited first.
During remodelling it is progressively replaced by type I, raising tensile strength.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Fresh wounds are weak because early collagen is type III.

mcqs.stem: Approximately what proportion of final strength has a wound regained at 3 weeks?

options.why: Classic figure: ~20% at 3 weeks.
Overestimates early strength.
80% is the figure at 3 months, not 3 weeks.
A wound never regains full original strength.
Underestimates 3-week strength.

explanation: At 3 weeks a wound has ~20% of final strength; at 3 months ~80% of original.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Remember 20-at-3-weeks, 80-at-3-months.

mcqs.stem: A contaminated laceration is left open for 5 days and then sutured because it looks clean. This is healing by:

options.why: Delayed primary closure of a contaminated wound after ~5 days is tertiary intention.
Primary intention closes a clean wound immediately, not after a delay.
Secondary intention is left to granulate without surgical closure.
Not a recognised category.
Regeneration restores original tissue without scar; not applicable to a sutured skin wound.

explanation: Delayed primary (tertiary) closure suits a contaminated wound: leave open ~5 days, then suture if no infection.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Delay-then-close = tertiary intention.

mcqs.stem: A raised scar that extends well beyond the original wound margin and does not regress is best described as:

options.why: Keloids cross the original margin and do not regress.
Hypertrophic scars stay within the wound margin and may regress.
A contracture is a tightening across a joint, not a scar that overspills margins.
Atrophic scars are depressed, not raised and overgrown.
Overgrowth beyond the margin is abnormal.

explanation: Keloid extends beyond the wound and does not regress; hypertrophic stays within and may regress.
keyFacts: Keloid crosses the margin; hypertrophic is held within.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Cross the margin = keloid.

mcqs.stem: Which single factor here most directly impairs healing?

options.why: Steroids impair the inflammatory/proliferative response and collagen synthesis.
Adequate protein and vitamins aid, not impair, healing.
Immobilisation actually protects granulation tissue.
Younger age favours healing; the elderly heal more slowly.
Good blood supply speeds healing.

explanation: Steroids, chemotherapy and immunosuppressants are the classic drug impairers of healing.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Steroids blunt inflammation and collagen synthesis.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about immobilisation and wound healing is correct?

options.text: Immobilisation aids healing by protecting granulation tissue
options.why: Movement/shear damages the granulation blood supply, so rest helps.

options.text: Immobilisation harms healing by reducing blood flow
options.why: It is movement, not rest, that damages granulation.

options.text: Movement improves healing by stimulating collagen
options.why: Shear injures the fragile granulation supply.

options.text: Immobilisation has no effect on healing
options.why: It has a definite protective effect locally.
Local mechanical factors matter too.

explanation: Immobilisation protects granulation tissue; shear from movement damages its blood supply.
mcqs.teachingPoint: A classic catch — immobilisation helps.

mcqs.stem: Which vitamin deficiency most specifically impairs protocollagen maturation?

options.why: Vitamin C is required for collagen (protocollagen) hydroxylation/maturation.
Vitamin A supports epithelialisation, a different step.
Vitamin K concerns clotting factors, not collagen maturation.
Vitamin D governs calcium/bone, not collagen cross-linking here.
B12 relates to haematopoiesis/neurology, not collagen maturation.

explanation: Vitamin C is needed for protocollagen maturation; vitamin A aids epithelialisation.
keyFacts: Vit C → collagen; Vit A → epithelium.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Scurvy impairs collagen and wound strength.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following are growth factors involved in wound healing? (Select all that apply.)

options.why: Platelet-derived growth factor is released early and recruits fibroblasts.
Tumour necrosis factor-α is part of the inflammatory signalling.
Interleukin-1 is an inflammatory mediator of healing.
Fibroblast growth factor drives fibroblast/endothelial activity.
Insulin is a metabolic hormone, not listed among the healing growth factors.

explanation: The chapter lists PDGF, TNF-α, IL-1 and FGF as growth factors of healing.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Know the four named growth factors.

mcqs.stem: Which phase of healing lasts approximately 5 days and features macrophage debridement?

options.why: The inflammatory phase runs ~5 days with macrophage debridement and growth-factor release.
Proliferation follows, forming granulation and epithelium.
Remodelling takes ~1 year.
Contraction is a component, not the ~5-day inflammatory phase.
A component of proliferation, not the inflammatory phase.

explanation: Haemostasis & inflammation ≈ 5 days; macrophages debride and release growth factors.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Macrophage is the key inflammatory-phase cell.

mcqs.stem: Roughly how long does the maturation & remodelling phase continue?

options.why: Remodelling continues for approximately a year as collagen realigns.
That is the inflammatory phase.
That is the time to epithelialise a clean sutured wound.
3 weeks is when ~20% strength is reached, not the end of remodelling.
Overstates the usual remodelling period.

explanation: Remodelling runs ~1 year; fibres thicken and align to lines of stress.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Scar keeps maturing for about a year.

mcqs.stem: A wound that is deeper than it is long, with a small skin opening, is a:

options.why: Penetrating wounds are deeper than long with poor drainage; suspect a hidden visceral injury.
Incised wounds are longer than deep with clean edges.
An abrasion is a superficial friction injury.
A contusion is a closed blunt injury with capillary extravasation.
A laceration is irregular and devascularised, not specifically deeper-than-long.

explanation: Penetrating = deeper than long; small opening → poor drainage and possible missed viscus.
keyFacts: Penetrating wound is deeper than long.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Depth > length → look deeper.

mcqs.stem: Regarding missile injuries, which factor contributes most to tissue damage?

options.why: KE = MV²/2g, so velocity (squared) dominates energy transfer.
Mass matters, but velocity is squared and dominates.
Irrelevant to energy transfer.
Entry size poorly predicts internal damage.
Not a determinant of missile energy.

explanation: Kinetic energy = MV²/2g; velocity is squared, so high-velocity rifles are far more destructive than pistols.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Velocity, squared, drives wounding energy.

mcqs.stem: A small, fluctuant collection of blood after blunt trauma is best managed initially by:

options.why: A small haematoma can be aspirated with a wide-bore needle.
Reserved for large haematomas.
Unnecessary and destructive for a small haematoma.
Aspiration is the described first step for a small collection.
Does not evacuate the collection.

explanation: Small haematoma → wide-bore needle aspiration; large → surgical evacuation under asepsis.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Size decides aspirate vs evacuate.

mcqs.stem: Which wound type is typically the most heavily contaminated and devascularised?

options.why: Blunt violence/RTA produces irregular, devascularised, contaminated tissue with high infection risk.
Incised wounds are clean-edged with little tissue destruction.
Superficial and generally not devascularised.
Made under asepsis, minimally contaminated.
A closed injury, not an open contaminated wound.

explanation: Lacerated wounds are irregular, devascularised and contaminated; oedema raises tension → ischaemia.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Lacerations carry the highest infection risk of the open wounds listed.

mcqs.stem: Why is an abrasion characteristically very painful?

options.why: Superficial scraping exposes cutaneous nerve endings.
Abrasions are superficial, not deep arterial injuries.
Abrasions do not reach bone.
Nerves are exposed, not necessarily transected as in incised wounds.
Not a feature of a superficial abrasion.

explanation: Abrasions scrape away superficial layers, exposing nerve endings → marked pain.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Superficial but very painful.

mcqs.stem: In a heavily contaminated limb wound, which actions are correct at first surgery? (Select all that apply.)

options.why: Contaminated wounds: leave the deep fascia open.

options.text: Do not close the skin primarily
options.why: Skin should not be closed primarily in a contaminated wound.
Tendon repair is deferred in contaminated wounds.
Nerve repair is deferred in contaminated wounds; repair clean incised wounds instead.
Necrotic muscle (dark, non-contractile, non-bleeding) is excised.

explanation: Contaminated-wound rule: no nerve/tendon repair, leave fascia and skin open, and excise dead muscle.
keyFacts: No nerve/tendon repair; fascia + skin open; excise dead muscle.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Deferring repair in contaminated wounds is correct, not negligent.

mcqs.stem: During debridement, which finding indicates muscle that should be excised?

options.text: No bleeding when cut and no contraction when pinched
options.why: Dark red/grey, non-contractile, non-bleeding muscle is dead and must be excised.
These indicate viable muscle to preserve.
Suggests viable, well-perfused muscle.
Not one of the four classic viability signs.
Not part of the described criteria.

explanation: Dead muscle: dark red/grey, no contraction when pinched, no bleeding when cut.
keyFacts: 4 Cs of dead muscle: colour, contractility, consistency, capacity to bleed.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Non-contractile, non-bleeding muscle is dead.

mcqs.stem: An open fracture with a high infection risk is best stabilised by:

options.why: External fixation avoids seeding metalwork into potentially infected bone.
Internal fixation risks spreading infection to bone.
Also internal metalwork — risks deep bone infection.
The fracture still needs stabilisation.
Not the described management of an infected-risk open fracture.

explanation: Use external fixation when infection risk is high; internal fixation could spread infection to bone.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Keep metal out of contaminated bone.

mcqs.stem: What is the correct first-aid method to control external haemorrhage from an open wound?

options.text: Direct compression with a sterile dressing
options.why: Direct compression is first-line; a tourniquet is only a temporary bridge to theatre.

options.text: Immediate proximal tourniquet as definitive care
options.why: A tourniquet is temporary only, not definitive.
Risks damaging nerves/vessels.
Insufficient for significant bleeding without compression.
Do not stop bleeding.

explanation: Stop bleeding by direct compression; reserve the tourniquet as a temporary measure before theatre.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Press first, tourniquet only to buy time.

mcqs.stem: A stab wound to the femoral triangle mandates particular concern for injury to which structures?

options.why: Timing and site predict injured structures; a femoral-triangle stab risks the femoral vessels.
That is in the arm, not the femoral triangle.
A neck structure, not the femoral triangle.
The popliteal fossa is behind the knee, not the femoral triangle.
An abdominal structure, unrelated to a thigh stab.

explanation: Ask timing and cause to predict injured structures; a femoral-triangle stab endangers the femoral vessels.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Anatomy of the wound predicts what is hurt.

mcqs.stem: What is the commonest type of chronic leg ulcer?

options.why: Venous ulcers are the commonest chronic leg ulcer.
Important but less common than venous.
Common in diabetes but not the commonest leg ulcer overall.
Uncommon (e.g. SCC in a chronic ulcer).
Not the commonest chronic leg ulcer category.

explanation: The commonest chronic leg ulcer is venous.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Think venous first for a chronic leg ulcer.

mcqs.stem: A pressure sore with full-thickness skin loss that stops short of the fascia is which stage?

options.why: Stage 3 = full-thickness skin loss short of fascia.
Stage 1 is erythema only.
Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss.
Stage 4 involves muscle, bone or joints.
There is no stage 5 in this scheme.

explanation: Stages: 1 erythema → 2 partial-thickness → 3 full-thickness short of fascia → 4 muscle/bone/joint.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Depth defines pressure-sore stage.

mcqs.stem: Which malignancy most classically develops within a long-standing chronic ulcer?

options.why: SCC is the classic malignant change in a chronic ulcer (a Marjolin-type ulcer).
Possible but rare compared with SCC.
Not the classic ulcer-related malignancy here.
Not the described association.
A bone tumour, not a chronic-ulcer skin malignancy.

explanation: Chronic leg ulcers may be neoplastic — usually SCC, rarely BCC.
mcqs.teachingPoint: A non-healing ulcer can harbour SCC.

mcqs.stem: Which is a recognised classic site for a pressure sore?

options.why: A classic pressure-sore site along with sacrum, greater trochanter, heel and malleoli.
Not a typical pressure-bearing site in a bedridden patient.
Not a pressure-sore site.
Not a classic decubitus site.
Not a listed pressure point.

explanation: Sites: ischial tuberosity, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleoli.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Pressure sores sit over bony prominences.

mcqs.stem: A wound that remains unhealed at roughly which time is defined as chronic?

options.why: A chronic wound fails the acute sequence within ~3 months.
Far too short to define chronicity.
This is when a wound has ~20% strength, not the chronicity threshold.
Overstates the threshold.
Not the figure given for chronicity.

explanation: Chronic wounds fail to heal within a reasonable time (~3 months), arrested at inflammatory/proliferative phases.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Three months marks chronicity.

mcqs.stem: What is the single most important way to classify a suture material?

options.why: Absorption is stated as the most important classifier.
Colour aids handling but is not the key classifier.
Irrelevant to the classification scheme.
A property of the needle, not the suture classification.
Not a classification of the material.

explanation: Sutures are classified by origin, synthesis and — most importantly — absorption.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Absorbable vs non-absorbable first.

mcqs.stem: Which is the slowest-absorbing absorbable suture?

options.why: PDS is the slowest absorbable; it loses ~50% tensile strength at 6 weeks.
Absorbed in ~3 weeks — fast.
Absorbed in 2–3 months, faster than PDS.
Absorption ~4 months, but PDS lasts longest.
Silk is classed non-absorbable (though slowly absorbable in fact).

explanation: PDS (polydioxanone) is the slowest-absorbing absorbable suture.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Choose PDS when prolonged support is needed.

mcqs.stem: Which suture is considered ideal for abdominal wall closure and hernia repair?

options.why: Monofilament and inert; ideal for abdominal closure and hernia repair.
Provokes marked reaction; must be removed if infected.
Absorbs too quickly and reacts.
Absorbable; used for GI anastomoses, not durable abdominal closure.
Reserved for sternotomy; difficult handling for abdominal closure.

explanation: Prolene is inert, monofilament and ideal for abdominal closure and hernia repair.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Inert monofilament suits the abdominal wall.

mcqs.stem: Compared with an equivalent monofilament, a multifilament (braided) suture picks up approximately how many more organisms?

options.why: Capillary spaces between filaments harbour bacteria — roughly 10× more.
Braided sutures harbour markedly more bacteria.
The opposite is true.
Overstates the figure given (~10×).
Understates the ~10× figure.

explanation: Multifilament sutures pick up ~10× more organisms than an equivalent monofilament.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Braid harbours bacteria in capillary spaces.

mcqs.stem: Which suture is used to close a sternotomy?

options.why: Very high tensile strength and very inert — used for sternotomy closure.
Ideal for abdominal closure, not the standard sternal wire.
Absorbable; unsuitable for sternal fixation.
Good tensile strength but not the sternotomy material.
Absorbs quickly; wholly unsuitable.

explanation: Stainless steel closes a sternotomy: very high tensile strength, very inert.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Sternum → steel.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about silk is the classic exam catch?

options.text: It is listed non-absorbable but is in fact very slowly absorbable
options.why: Silk sits in the non-absorbable list yet is slowly absorbable and provokes marked reaction.

options.text: It is fully inert like steel
options.why: Silk is protein and provokes marked tissue reaction.
Silk is multifilament (braided).

options.text: It should never be removed if infected
options.why: Silk should be removed if the wound is infected.

options.text: It is the strongest suture available
options.why: Not its defining feature; steel has very high tensile strength.

explanation: Silk is classed non-absorbable but is slowly absorbable and highly reactive; remove if infected.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Silk is the exam trap in the suture list.

mcqs.stem: In which situation is an occlusive dressing contraindicated?

options.why: Occlusive dressings are unsuitable for infected or highly exudative wounds.
A reasonable use for an occlusive dressing.

options.text: A wound needing a moist environment
options.why: Occlusion maintains hydration — appropriate here.
Not a contraindication.
Not contraindicated for a clean minor abrasion.

explanation: Occlusive dressings maintain hydration and autolysis but are not for infected or highly exudative wounds.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Don't seal an infected or weepy wound.

mcqs.stem: VAC (negative-pressure) therapy promotes healing chiefly by:

options.why: Negative pressure boosts granulation and contraction; useful in bed sores and diabetic ulcers.
It does not sterilise the wound.
Debridement is still needed; VAC complements it.
VAC is a topical negative-pressure device, not a drug route.
Not its mechanism.

explanation: VAC applies negative pressure → more granulation and contraction; good in bed sores and diabetic ulcers.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Negative pressure grows granulation tissue.

mcqs.stem: Which dressing is seaweed-derived and forms a gel on contact with exudate?

options.why: Alginates are seaweed-derived and gel with exudate.
A semi-occlusive dressing giving a moist bed, not seaweed-derived gel.
A simple occlusive material, not a gelling alginate.
An osmotic agent, not an alginate.
A semi-permeable film, not an alginate.

explanation: Alginates come from seaweed and form a fibrous gel with exudate.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Alginate suits exudative wounds.

mcqs.stem: A semi-occlusive dressing is characterised by being:

options.text: Permeable to gases/vapour but impermeable to bacteria
options.why: Semi-occlusive dressings let vapour and gases through but keep bacteria out.
That describes a fully occlusive dressing.
They are specifically impermeable to bacteria.
Not their defining feature.
That describes alginate dressings.

explanation: Semi-occlusive: permeable to water vapour/gases, impermeable to bacteria (e.g. hydrocolloid).
mcqs.teachingPoint: Breathable but a bacterial barrier.

mcqs.stem: What single measure is most central to preventing further pressure sores in such a patient?

options.why: Relieving sustained pressure by regular turning is central; support surfaces and nutrition also help.
Antibiotics treat infection but do not prevent pressure necrosis.
Immobility without turning worsens pressure sores.
Occlusion is wrong for an exudative/infected deep sore and does not offload pressure.
Massaging established sores is not the described preventive measure.

explanation: Prevention centres on relieving pressure (regular turning), correcting general factors, air mattresses and skin care.
keyFacts: Turn the patient to offload pressure.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Pressure relief prevents pressure sores.

mcqs.stem: What is the most accurate answer about its ultimate strength?

options.text: It will never regain full original strength
options.why: A healed wound never returns to 100% of original tensile strength.

options.text: It is already at full strength by 3 weeks
options.why: Only ~20% of final strength is present at 3 weeks.

options.text: It reaches full strength at 3 months
options.why: ~80% of original at 3 months, not 100%.

options.text: It reaches full strength at 1 year
options.why: Remodelling continues ~1 year but never reaches 100%.
Tensile strength continues to rise long after epithelial cover.

explanation: A wound gains ~20% strength at 3 weeks and ~80% at 3 months, and never regains full original strength.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Scar is permanently weaker than intact skin.

mcqs.stem: Which mechanism best explains damage remote from the visible track?

options.why: High-velocity rounds create a temporary cavity and shock waves damaging tissue beyond the track.
Direct track injury alone cannot explain remote damage.
Not the described mechanism of remote injury.
Not the acute wounding mechanism here.
Infection is a later complication, not the immediate remote damage.

explanation: High-velocity missiles damage tissue by track injury, shock waves, temporary cavitation and secondary bone fragments.
keyFacts: Cavitation damages tissue away from the track.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Small holes can hide huge internal cavitation.

mcqs.stem: Which management combination is most appropriate?

options.text: Debride, leave fascia and skin open, plan delayed primary closure, give tetanus + anaerobic cover
options.why: Contaminated/late wounds: debride, leave open, delayed primary closure, tetanus and anaerobic prophylaxis.

options.text: Primary closure of skin and fascia now
options.why: Primary closure is wrong for a contaminated, late wound.
These repairs are deferred in contaminated wounds.
Internal fixation risks spreading infection to bone.
Both closing skin and withholding prophylaxis are wrong here.

explanation: Late contaminated wound: debride, leave fascia/skin open, delayed primary closure, tetanus prophylaxis and anaerobic cover.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Never close a dirty, late wound primarily.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a NON-absorbable suture?

options.why: Prolene is non-absorbable and inert.
PDS is absorbable (the slowest).
Vicryl is absorbable.
Catgut is absorbable.
Dexon is absorbable.

explanation: Prolene is non-absorbable; PDS, Vicryl, Dexon and catgut are absorbable.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Sort sutures by absorption first.

mcqs.stem: Which agents act as osmotic dressings that draw down exudate?

options.why: Honey is listed as an osmotic agent that absorbs exudate.
Urea crystals act osmotically to absorb exudate.
Debrisan is an osmotic agent.
Alginate gels with exudate but is classed separately, not as an osmotic agent.
A semi-occlusive dressing, not an osmotic agent.

explanation: Osmotic agents — Debrisan, urea crystals and honey — absorb exudate.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Osmotic dressings pull fluid out of the wound.

mcqs.stem: Which sequence correctly orders pressure-sore stages by increasing depth?

options.text: Erythema → partial-thickness → full-thickness short of fascia → muscle/bone
options.why: This is the correct staging order 1→4.
Out of order.
Reversed order.
Erythema is stage 1, before partial-thickness.
Muscle involvement is the deepest stage, not second.

explanation: Stages progress 1 erythema → 2 partial-thickness → 3 full-thickness short of fascia → 4 muscle/bone/joint.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Stage rises with depth.

mcqs.stem: Which is the correct order of the phases of wound healing?

options.why: The phases run inflammation → proliferation → remodelling.
Inflammation comes first.
Reversed order.
Inflammation is first, not last.
Proliferation precedes maturation.

explanation: Order: haemostasis & inflammation → proliferation → maturation & remodelling (HIP-R).
mcqs.teachingPoint: Inflammation always leads.

mcqs.stem: A patient with a limb wound has absent distal pulses. What is the most appropriate immediate investigation?

options.why: Absent distal pulses demand urgent duplex to assess vascular injury.
Too slow for a limb-threatening vascular concern.
X-ray addresses fracture, not the absent pulse.
Absent pulses are an emergency, not for observation.
Irrelevant to acute vascular assessment.

explanation: Feel distal pulses; if absent, arrange urgent duplex ultrasound.
mcqs.teachingPoint: No pulse = urgent vascular imaging.

emqs.instruction: For each description, select the single most appropriate wound type.

stems.stem: A clean-edged wound from a knife that is longer than it is deep, bleeding briskly.
stems.why: A sharp edge gives clean margins with little tissue destruction and free bleeding.

stems.stem: A wound from a pointed nail that is deeper than it is long, with a small skin opening and poor drainage.
stems.why: Penetrating wounds are deeper than long; the small opening drains poorly and hides deep injury.

stems.stem: A collection of blood under intact skin that becomes cystic then clots within hours.
stems.why: A haematoma is a discrete blood collection; small ones can be aspirated with a wide-bore needle.

stems.stem: Superficial layers scraped away by friction, exposing many nerve endings and very painful.
stems.why: Abrasions are painful because superficial nerve endings are exposed; clean and dress non-adherently.

stems.stem: An irregular, devascularised, contaminated wound from a road-traffic blunt injury.
stems.why: Blunt violence tears tissue irregularly, leaving devascularised contaminated edges at high infection risk.

keyFacts: Deeper-than-long = penetrating; longer-than-deep with clean edges = incised.
Missile severity scales with kinetic energy (½MV²).

emqs.instruction: For each property, select the single most appropriate suture.

stems.stem: Inert monofilament that need not be removed even if the wound becomes infected; ideal for abdominal closure and hernia repair.
stems.why: Prolene is inert and monofilament, so it does not harbour organisms and can stay in an infected field.

stems.stem: The slowest-absorbed synthetic, a monofilament losing about half its tensile strength at six weeks.
stems.why: PDS is a monofilament absorbable with the longest wound support of the absorbables.

stems.stem: Braided absorbable synthetic commonly chosen for gastrointestinal anastomoses.
stems.why: Vicryl (polyglactin) is a multifilament absorbable widely used for bowel anastomoses.

stems.stem: Very high tensile strength and very inert but hard to handle; used for sternotomy closure.
stems.why: Stainless steel is the strongest and most inert suture, used to close the sternum.

stems.stem: A natural protein multifilament that provokes marked tissue reaction and should be removed if infected.
stems.why: Silk handles easily but its protein multifilament structure reacts and can maintain infection.

keyFacts: Multifilament sutures pick up ~10× more organisms than an equivalent monofilament.
Absorbable vs non-absorbable is the single most important suture classification.
